# 1 Samuel 30 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into six sections: (1) the Amalekite raid on Ziklag (vv. 1–2); (2) David's distress and his strengthening himself in the LORD (vv. 3–6); (3) David's inquiry of the LORD via the ephod (vv. 7–8); (4) the pursuit, the exhausted 200, and the finding of the Egyptian slave (vv. 9–15); (5) the victory and total recovery (vv. 16–20); (6) the distribution of spoil — to the 200 who stayed, and to the elders of Judah (vv. 21–31).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

---

## v. 1 — David returns to find Ziklag burned

**Traditional Reading:** David and his men took three days to march roughly 25 miles per day from Aphek (1 Samuel 29:11) back to Ziklag. They arrived tired and expecting home comforts. The Amalekites had exploited David's absence (he was away trying to join the Philistine army) and raided the Negev and Ziklag, burning it. This was a retaliatory strike, since David had raided Amalekite territory earlier (1 Samuel 27:8).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html (Constable)

**Poetic Justice / Providence:** Enduring Word notes a "touch of the LORD's poetic justice" — David had brought the same calamity (burning towns, taking captives, though he killed everyone) on other cities during his Philistine sojourn. The Amalekites were actually *more merciful* than David had been, since they killed no one. God tempers discipline with mercy.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Precept Austin** adds that David was reaping consequences on three levels: (a) Saul's failure to destroy the Amalekites in 1 Samuel 15; (b) David's own raids that provoked revenge; (c) David's compromise in allying with the Philistines.  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary

---

## v. 2 — Women and all taken captive, none killed

**Traditional Reading:** The Amalekites took captive women and children "from small to great" but killed no one. This was remarkable for a revenge raid, and preachers see the hand of God preserving life. Had they massacred the families, David's future reign would have begun under a far darker cloud.  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Gill** notes simply that the Amalekites "carried them off and went their way," intending to sell them as slaves or keep them.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-30.html

---

## v. 3 — David and his men discover the burned city and captive families

**Traditional Reading:** The sight of smoke from a distance, then the silent, burned-out ghost town, turned the soldiers' homecoming joy into horror. The writer repeats the key facts (city burned, families gone but alive) to underscore the shock. David and his men would have searched the ruins for bones or remains and found none — a sign of God's mercy even in judgment.  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

---

## v. 4 — David and his men weep until exhausted

**Traditional Reading:** These were hardened warriors, yet they "lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep." The phrase suggests prolonged, exhausting grief — perhaps hours of wailing. They were physically drained from the march and now emotionally crushed.

**Spurgeon:** "Weary with their marching, they had hoped to rest at home; but now that everything was gone, the strong men, who were not often moved to weeping, wept till they could weep no longer; the very sources of tears were dried up by the exceeding heat of their grief."  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary (quoting Spurgeon)

**Constable** sees this as an example of David's empathy — he wept *with* his men, sharing their grief rather than standing apart.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

---

## v. 5 — David's two wives taken

**Traditional Reading:** Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail (widow of Nabal) are named. The narrator singles out David's personal loss. Commentators note David apparently had no children yet at this time (unlike his men). The thought of what captors might do to Abigail would have tormented him.  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary

---

## v. 6 — David greatly distressed; men speak of stoning him; he strengthens himself in the LORD

**This is the theological heart of the chapter.**

**Traditional Reading (all traditions agree on the core):** David hit rock bottom. His city was ashes, his family gone, his own men — bitter over their lost children — talked of stoning him. Every earthly support was stripped away. "But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God." This is the turning point.

**Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist):** Devoted an entire sermon ("Ziklag; or, David Encouraging Himself in God," No. 1606, 1881) to vv. 6–8. He emphasised: (a) David's distress was self-inflicted — he had been acting without consulting God, living by policy and deceit among the Philistines, and this disaster was God's cure. (b) David "encouraged himself" — he didn't wait for someone else to do it. "Some of the best talks in the world are those which a man has with himself." (c) He encouraged himself *in the Lord*, not in his new allies from Manasseh (1 Chronicles 12:19–20), not in positive thinking, but by remembering God's love, God's calling on his life, and God's past deliverances (lion, bear, Goliath, Saul's pursuit). (d) Even a backslidden sinner can and must run *toward* God, not away from Him. "When he lifts his arm, as it were, to execute vengeance, lay hold upon it and he will spare you."  
— https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/ziklag-or-david-encouraging-himself-in-god

**Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Emphasises that David was "completely broken, ready to be filled." David's backslidden state made this moment of strengthening all the more remarkable — it was pure grace. David did not passively wait; he actively took hold of God's strength by remembering God's love (the Philistine rejection that sent him home was actually God's kindness), God's promise and calling, and God's past deliverances.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Gill (older Baptist):** "David encouraged himself in the Lord his God; took all patiently, and exercised faith on his God; he encouraged himself in the power and providence of God; in the promises of God, and his faithfulness in keeping them; in a view of his covenant relation to God; in remembrance of the grace, mercy, and goodness of God, and his former experiences of it." The Targum reads: "he strengthened himself in the Word of the Lord his God" — i.e., in Christ the Word.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-30.html

**Ellicott (Anglican):** "He encouraged himself in prayer, thus casting himself and his fortunes on the God who, years before, had chosen him to be 'His anointed.'" Ellicott contrasts David's trust with Saul's despair at Endor.  
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/30.htm

**Constable (Evangelical/DTS):** "David's genius was his spiritual resilience." From the Psalms we know David did this by looking back on God's past faithfulness, looking up in prayer, and looking forward with God's promises in view.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

**James Smith / Handfuls of Purpose (via Precept Austin):** "David now comes to himself, and turns to the Lord as unto a friend in the time of need… The spirit of faith again sits on the throne of David's heart, as when he faced Goliath."  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary

**Ray Pritchard (via Precept Austin):** Notes that for 16 months among the Philistines there are no recorded prayers or psalms from David. "Ziklag is burning and it's all David's fault. What started with discouragement led to desperation which led to defection which led to disobedience which culminated in disaster."  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary

---

## vv. 7–8 — David inquires of the LORD via the ephod; God answers

**Traditional Reading:** Having strengthened himself inwardly, David now acts. For the first time during his Philistine sojourn, he inquires of the LORD. He summons Abiathar the priest and asks for the ephod — almost certainly the high priest's ephod containing the Urim and Thummim (the "breastplate of judgment," Exodus 28:15–30). David asks two precise questions: "Shall I pursue? Will I overtake them?" God answers both: "Pursue, for you shall surely overtake them and rescue (without fail recover all)."

**Enduring Word:** God gave David something to *do* (pursue) and a *promise* in the doing. The promise did not exclude David's cooperation — it invited it. Also notes that David, now returning from backsliding, brought *everything* to the LORD; nothing was assumed.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Spurgeon:** "David wisely stops. 'Bring hither the ephod,' cries he, and he waits till the oracle answers his enquiries. He will not march till the Lord shall give the word of command." David takes it for granted that God will help; he only wants to know *how*. And he does not expect God to help without his own effort — "Shall I pursue? shall I overtake?" — he means to act.  
— https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/ziklag-or-david-encouraging-himself-in-god

**Gill:** Notes that David inquired *through* Abiathar, who reported the questions in David's name. God's answer "without fail recover all" goes beyond what David asked (he asked only about overtaking, not about recovering).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-30.html

**Ellicott** has an extended excursus on the Urim and Thummim, describing the high priest's breastplate and the various theories of how the oracle functioned (by the engraved divine name, by prophetic voice, etc.).  
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/30.htm

---

## vv. 9–10 — The march to the Brook Besor; 200 stay behind

**Traditional Reading:** David leads all 600 men out. At the Brook Besor (probably Wadi el-Arish, the southwestern border of the promised land), 200 are too exhausted to cross. David leaves them to guard the supplies and presses on with 400.

**Spurgeon:** "When God means to bless us, he often takes away a part of the little strength we thought we had. Our God does not fill till he has emptied." The reduction from 600 to 400 was a further trial of faith — but God meant the 400 to match the 400 Amalekites who would later flee on camels (v. 17), making the victory clearly God's doing.  
— https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/ziklag-or-david-encouraging-himself-in-god

**Enduring Word:** David didn't let this discouragement stop him. He set the 200 to useful work (guarding supplies) and continued in faith.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Constable:** Notes the parallel with 1 Samuel 25:13 (David dividing his men when facing Nabal), part of a larger pattern of contrasts between wise David and foolish Nabal in these chapters.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

---

## vv. 11–12 — The Egyptian slave found and revived

**Traditional Reading:** David's men find an Egyptian collapsed in a field. They give him bread, water, a fig cake, and two clusters of raisins. He had eaten and drunk nothing for three days and three nights. His strength returns.

**Enduring Word:** David showed "unexpected kindness" when it would have been easy and "logical" to ignore this man because of the "greater mission." This kindness became the key to the entire victory. The episode is a picture of Christ, who "is not ashamed to pick up the world's sick and half-dead castaways."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Precept Austin / James Smith:** "This poor unfortunate youth… is the divinely-appointed means to the fulfilment of the God-given promise. The means are in His hand as well as the end; and the things that God chooses are 'weak and despised'… like this dying Egyptian, but mighty to the pulling down of the strongholds of Satan (1 Cor. 1:27, 28)."  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary

**Constable:** Contrasts David's kindness to this Egyptian with his earlier plan to slaughter Nabal and all his household (ch. 25) — evidence of growth in David's restraint. Also contrasts the Amalekite master's heartless abandonment of his sick slave with David's compassionate care.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

---

## vv. 13–15 — The Egyptian's story; he agrees to guide David

**Traditional Reading:** The Egyptian reveals he is the slave of an Amalekite who abandoned him when he fell ill three days earlier. He confesses he participated in the raids: "We raided the Negev of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag." David asks him to lead them to the raiders. The Egyptian agrees on condition that David swears by God not to kill him or return him to his master.

**Enduring Word:** "The emphatic 'we'… suggests that the slave participated personally in the Amalekites' raids" (citing Youngblood).  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Constable:** The Egyptian's request for an oath of safety mirrors Saul's request in 1 Samuel 24:2. David grants it, winning his cooperation.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

---

## vv. 16–17 — The Amalekites surprised and slaughtered

**Traditional Reading:** The Egyptian leads David to the Amalekite camp. They are "spread out over all the land, eating, drinking, and celebrating" — feasting on their plunder, confident that all armies were far north. David attacks "from twilight until the evening of the next day."

**Twilight or Dawn?** Enduring Word (citing Baldwin) argues "twilight" is a poor translation: the Hebrew *nesep* means "dawn" (as in Job 7:4; Psalm 119:147). David and his men rested overnight, observed the Amalekites' drunken feasting, and attacked at first light when they were hungover and vulnerable. Trapp: "Whom they found it no hard matter to stab with the sword, who were cup-shot before."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Constable:** The battle lasted from early morning until nightfall. Only 400 young men escaped on camels — meaning the Amalekite force far outnumbered David's 400. Camels were the fastest transport of the era (cf. Judges 7:12).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

---

## vv. 18–19 — David recovers everything

**Traditional Reading:** "David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives. Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder." God's promise in v. 8 ("without fail recover all") was fulfilled exactly.

**Enduring Word:** The promise was fulfilled, but *through* David's action, not despite it. "God's promise didn't exclude David's cooperation, the promise invited his cooperation." Spurgeon: "Brother, you will have to work and labour to extricate yourself from debt and difficulty, and so the Lord will hear your prayer."  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Precept Austin / James Smith:** "A Complete Victory. 'David recovered all.' … What a prefiguring of Him who was David's Lord, and who encouraged Himself in His God, and came forth to recover all that was lost through the sinful failure of the first Adam."  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary

---

## v. 20 — "This is David's plunder!"

**Traditional Reading:** Beyond recovering what was taken from Ziklag, David also captured the Amalekites' own flocks and herds — spoil *beyond* what God had promised. The men drove these ahead, calling out "This is David's plunder!" (or "This is David's spoil").

**Enduring Word:** This was "a blessing straight from the grace of God." It also addresses why David could keep Amalekite spoil when Saul was condemned for doing the same (1 Samuel 15): (a) David had no specific command to destroy everything; (b) David was recovering what was taken from others, plus extra; (c) David was not acting as king representing the nation in holy war, as Saul was.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

---

## vv. 21–22 — David greets the 200; the "wicked and worthless" protest

**Traditional Reading:** David returns to the 200 at the Brook Besor and greets them warmly. But "all the wicked and worthless men" among the 400 fighters protest: the 200 who stayed behind may have their wives and children back, but no share of the plunder.

**Enduring Word:** Identifies these protesters as *some* among David's men (not all 400). Their attitude was selfish and failed to see that the victory was the LORD's doing.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Constable:** Notes David's habit of initiating friendly greeting (cf. 1 Samuel 17:22; 25:5–6) — a model for believers, as the NT frequently exhorts greeting one another.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

---

## vv. 23–25 — David's ruling: equal shares for all

**Traditional Reading:** David overrules the protesters with four arguments: (1) "My brothers" — he addresses them as family, not subordinates. (2) The plunder is "what the LORD has given us" — not what *we* won. (3) "He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders" — God, not human effort, secured victory. (4) "The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies." He makes this "a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this very day."

**Constable:** David's policy harmonised with the Mosaic Law (Numbers 31:27, which required dividing spoil between fighters and the congregation). His ruling "further prepared the way for the Judahites' acceptance of David as Saul's successor."  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

**Enduring Word:** The principle established is that "the hidden supporter is as valuable to God's victory as the visible warrior." The weary 200 who guarded supplies contributed genuinely to the mission.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Coffman:** Notes this statute endured "to this day" (the time of the writer), showing it became embedded in Israel's legal tradition.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-samuel-30.html

**Denominational distinctives:** No major tradition disputes the plain meaning here. The passage is often cited in discussions of fairness in ministry — those who "stay with the supplies" (prayer supporters, administrators, etc.) share equally in the reward with frontline workers.

---

## vv. 26–31 — David sends gifts to the elders of Judah

**Traditional Reading:** Back in Ziklag, David sends portions of the plunder to "his friends, the elders of Judah," calling it "a gift… from the plunder of the LORD's enemies." He sends to at least 13 named locations: Bethel, Ramoth Negev, Jattir, Aroer, Siphmoth, Eshtemoa, Racal, cities of the Jerahmeelites and Kenites, Hormah, Bor-ashan, Athach, and Hebron — "all the places where David and his men had roamed."

**Constable:** David did this (a) because he viewed the plunder as belonging to all Judah — it was from "the LORD's enemies"; (b) to express gratitude to those who sheltered him during his fugitive years; and (c) politically, to curry favour with those who would soon anoint him king (2 Samuel 2:4; 5:1–3). "David's propensity to give made his new kingdom possible."  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

**Enduring Word:** This act prefigures Christ's distribution of the spoils of His victory to His friends. Christ gives gifts to His people from what He won at the cross.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

**Gill:** "Spoil of the enemies of the LORD" is a telling phrase — David frames the Amalekites not merely as his own enemies but as *God's* enemies, making the gift a sacred matter.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-30.html

**Precept Austin / James Smith:** "He who 'recovered all' now offers a blessing to all his friends. … He shall divide the spoil of His unsearchable riches with the strong in faith (Isa. 53:12)."  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-30-commentary

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

I was unable to fetch separate pages for each tradition, but the searches indicate broad agreement on this chapter's main themes. Some nuances:

- **Reformed Baptist (Spurgeon):** Heavy emphasis on divine sovereignty in David's distress — God *sent* the trial to cure David of self-reliance and deceit. The strengthening is entirely Godward.  
  — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/ziklag-or-david-encouraging-himself-in-god

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises the active dimension — David "took hold" of God's strength; the promise required human cooperation; the fivefold typological picture of Christ (we are David's men, the weary, the Egyptian slave, the spoils recovered, and the elders receiving gifts).  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-30/

- **Evangelical/Dispensational (Constable, DTS):** Emphasises leadership qualities modelled by David, the narrative parallels with chapter 25 (Nabal contrast), and the political wisdom of David's gift-giving as preparation for kingship. Also stresses continuity with the Mosaic Law (Numbers 31:27).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-30.html

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Focus on the Urim and Thummim as the historical means of divine guidance and the contrast between David's faith and Saul's despair.  
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/30.htm
